title: Pollen from wetland of Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve regenerative capacity of tropical forest ecosystems
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 3:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A new study carried out at Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve shows that in 2700- and 2300-years BP, the region experienced a strong Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM), while between 2300- and 1600-years BP, it underwent multiple climatic phases, including periods of high humidity and prolonged drought significantly influencing the composition, structure, distribution of forest vegetation and shifts in regional landscape through time.
This was followed by stable monsoon and increasing evidence of human activity between 1600 and 820 years BP and strengthening of monsoons during the last 400 years resulting in recovery of forests.
This indicated the resilience and regenerative capacity of tropical forest ecosystems that populated the region, under favourable climatic conditions.
Understanding the long-term variability of the ISM is essential because it is a key driver of India's climate, ecosystems, and water resources. As Indian agriculture is highly dependent on monsoon rainfall, even small changes in monsoon intensity or timing can affect crop productivity, food security, and the national economy. Reconstructing past climate and vegetation changes provides valuable long-term insights into natural monsoon variability and ecosystem responses.
However, there is a lack of high-resolution Late Holocene palaeoclimate records from the Core Monsoon Zone (CMZ) of central India.
Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an Autonomous Institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), used pollen-based records from Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in central India's Core Monsoon Zone and integrated them with the Earth System Paleoclimate Simulation (ESPS) model to reconstruct vegetation and Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) variability over the past ~2700 years.
Fig 1
: Three-dimensional (3D) elevation model of the
Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve
, located in the Core Monsoon Zone, Madhya Pradesh, India.
This combination allowed researchers to reconstruct historical Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) patterns for the past 3000 years, correlating climate changes with significant events in Indian history.
Dr. Anjali Trivedi, along with Anupam Nag and Prof. M. G. Thakkar from BSIP) studied sediment core from the Chakradhara Wetland of Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve, located in Umaria district of Northeastern Madhya Pradesh, India, segmented the core and prepared samples for radio carbon dating and pollen analysis.
They also generated Earth System Palaeoclimate Simulation (ESPS) models to reconstruct climatic conditions over the past three millennia. These models were then used to compare the pollen dataset, ensuring the authenticity and reliability of the research findings.
They found that between approximately 2700- and 2300-years BP, a strengthened Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) supported widespread dense moist deciduous forests dominated by Sal (
Shorea robusta
). Its proliferation indicates sustained rainfall of around 1100–1200 mm or more annually, along with a timely monsoon onset.
Fig 2
: Digital elevation model (DEM) of the Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve showing the location of the study site in the Core Monsoon Zone, Madhya Pradesh, India.
Between around 2300- and 1600-years BP, the region experienced multiple climatic phases, including periods of high humidity, prolonged drought, gradual environmental recovery, and a subsequent strengthening of the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM). These climatic fluctuations significantly influenced the composition, structure, and distribution of forest vegetation, resulting in shifts in the regional landscape through time.
The period 1600 and 820 years BP saw relatively stable monsoon conditions supported dense tropical forests. From 820 to 400 years BP, weakening of the ISM led to reduced moist deciduous forests and expansion of dry deciduous vegetation, accompanied by increasing Cerealia and other cultivated pollen, indicating growing agricultural activity, land-use change and human influence.
Over the past ~400 years, strengthening monsoon conditions promoted the recovery and expansion of moist deciduous forests, demonstrating the resilience and regenerative capacity of tropical forest ecosystems under favourable climatic conditions.
The findings published in Quaternary Research can improve our understanding of climate–environment interactions and can contribute to better climate adaptation strategies, sustainable agriculture, and future climate resilience.

https://doi.org/10.1017/qua.2026.10093

Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, represented the Government of India as the Chief Guest at the National Day Reception of the Sultanate of Oman, hosted at the Embassy of the Sultanate of Oman in Chanakyapuri, New Delhi, today. Addressing the gathering, Sarbananda Sonowal extended warm greetings on behalf of the Government and the people of India to His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, the Government, and the friendly people of Oman, wishing the Sultanate continued peace, progress, and prosperity.
Underscoring the deep-rooted historical ties between the two nations, the Union Minister noted that for nearly five thousand years, sailors and merchants have crossed the Arabian Sea, connecting ancient Indian ports with Muscat, Sohar, and Salalah. “The Arabian Sea has never separated our countries. It has always connected us,” Sonowal said, adding that these centuries-old exchanges built bonds of trust long before formal diplomatic ties were established.
Recalling his visit to Muscat in January this year to welcome INSV Kaundinya following its maiden voyage from Porbandar, Sonowal described the vessel, inspired by a fifth-century ship depicted in the Ajanta caves and built using traditional stitching techniques, as a living symbol of the enduring maritime, trade, and people-to-people ties between India and Oman.
Highlighting the renewed momentum in the India-Oman Strategic Partnership following Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Oman in December 2025, Sonowal pointed to two landmark milestones: the entry into force of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) in June 2026, and the adoption of the
Joint Vision Document on Maritime Cooperation
.
“India and Oman are natural maritime partners occupying strategic positions along major shipping routes connecting Asia, Africa, and Europe. Oman’s ports at Duqm, Sohar, and Salalah, together with India’s expanding port network, can support stronger trade connectivity and more resilient supply chains,” the Union Minister stated. He emphasised vast opportunities for bilateral collaboration in port-led development, shipbuilding and ship repair, green fuels, digital port systems, maritime training, logistics, and the blue economy.
Sonowal also underscored the importance of maritime security and praised Oman’s balanced and constructive role in regional and international affairs. He expressed India’s deep gratitude to the Omani authorities for their consistent humanitarian assistance to Indian nationals, particularly Indian seafarers in distress.
Celebrating the human bridge between the two countries, Sonowal highlighted the contributions of nearly seven lakh Indians living in Oman and commended cultural preservation initiatives such as the book “Mandvi to Muscat” and the digitisation of thousands of historical records belonging to Indian families in Oman.
Emphasising the strong synergy between
Oman Vision 2040
and India’s
Viksit Bharat 2047
, Sonowal noted that under the leadership of His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the bilateral partnership stands as a model of trust, stability, and cooperation in the Indian Ocean region.
Concluding his address, the Union Minister reaffirmed India’s commitment to the enduring friendship, stating that shared history provides strong foundations, the sea offers a shared horizon, and mutual trust gives both nations the confidence to sail forward together.

title: Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Chairs Plenary Session of ‘SAMAVESHI NITI SANKALP 2026’
subtitle:
Calls For Whole-Of-Government Approach To Build An Inclusive, Accessible And Drug-Free India

Centre And States Identify Time-Bound Action Points On Drug Demand Reduction, Scholarships, Early Intervention And Accessibility; Summit Reinforces Collective Commitment Towards Viksit Bharat @2047
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 5:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi applauded the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for organizing the Departmental Summit and facilitating meaningful deliberations. The Prime Minister emphasized the importance of collective action and a ‘Whole of Government’ approach in achieving the objectives of social justice, social empowerment and a Nasha Mukt Bharat.
Addressing the
plenary session of the two-day Departmental Summit titled
‘Samaveshi Niti Sankalp’
, at the Sushma Swaraj Bhawan, in the National Capital here on Thursday, Shri Modi h
ighlighted the transformative impact of the Government’s welfare initiatives,
he observed that nearly 50 crore people lifted out of poverty have experienced genuine social empowerment.
Calling for the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan to be transformed into a nationwide
Jan Andolan
, the Prime Minister stressed that every citizen, family, educational institution and community must contribute to building a drug-free India.
Shri Modi encouraged schools to organize essay competitions and undertake awareness initiatives, while sensitizing parents to recognize early signs of substance abuse and addiction.
Emphasizing the importance of rehabilitation and social reintegration, the Prime Minister observed that the journeys of individuals who have successfully overcome substance dependence carry a powerful message of hope.
“These journeys carry the strongest message of hope. They show that recovery is possible and that a life free from drugs is a life of dignity,” he said.
The Prime Minister also urged farmers to shun illicit crop cultivation and called for coordinated efforts involving all Ministries, State Governments, district administrations and spiritual organizations to strengthen the national campaign against drug abuse.
Recognising the influence of spiritual leaders, the Prime Minister said that spiritual gurus and organisations have a vital role to play in the mission. Their guidance, he noted, can inspire millions to choose a life free from drugs.
On the empowerment of persons with disabilities, the Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the term ‘
Divyang’
, noting its contribution towards enhancing the dignity, respect and self-esteem of persons with disabilities.
Shri Modi encouraged its wider use and popularization to foster a positive outlook towards Divyangjan across society. He also emphasized the need to identify, nurture and recognize their inherent talents and abilities by providing appropriate opportunities and platforms for their participation and contribution.
The Prime Minister’s address reinforced the need for sustained cooperation between the Centre and States, institutional convergence and effective implementation of welfare programmes to ensure that the benefits of development reach every section of society.
The Summit was attended by Union Ministers for Social Justice and Empowerment, Ministers from 27 States and Union Territories, Secretaries of both Departments, Secretaries from 35 States and Union Territories, and senior officers of the Ministry and participating State/UT administrations, to deliberate on key priorities and strengthen collaborative efforts towards inclusive social development and empowerment.
Four thematic priorities deliberated at the Summit
The two-day Departmental Summit commenced on November 18, 2026, with the inaugural session addressed by Union Minister for Social Justice and Empowerment Dr. Virendra Kumar. Context-setting remarks were delivered by the Secretaries of the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment (DoSJE) and the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), outlining the policy priorities and implementation challenges relating to drug demand reduction, scholarships, early intervention and accessibility.
The first day featured four thematic deliberations focusing on
Re-imagining Prevention and Drug Demand Reduction for Nasha Mukt Bharat
;
Accessible Scholarships, Empowered Students
;
Early Intervention and Reduction of Disability Burden
; and
Sugamya Bharat for Viksit Bharat
.
Four parallel breakout sessions provided a platform for Ministers and senior officials from States and Union Territories to exchange best practices, discuss implementation challenges and identify actionable measures with clearly defined timelines.
1. Re-imagining Prevention and Drug Demand Reduction for Nasha Mukt Bharat
The session, chaired by Dr. (Col.) Dhani Ram Shandil, Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, Himachal Pradesh, and co-chaired by Shri Avinash Gehlot, Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, Rajasthan, focused on transforming drug prevention and awareness efforts into a sustained
Jan Andolan
.
The key action points included observing the 10th of every month as
Nasha Mukti Sankalp Diwas
, beginning December 2026; making drug prevention a standing agenda item in every Gram Sabha and Municipal Ward; and establishing at least one de-addiction centre in every district by March 2029.
States shared several innovative initiatives, including Chandigarh’s VADA Clubs, Punjab’s SOORMA Ambassadors, Meghalaya’s DREAM Solace Home, Jammu and Kashmir’s 100 Days Campaign and Haryana’s STARS Rating for rehabilitation centres.
Dr. Shandil underscored the importance of structured and continuous interventions through families, schools and communities, observing that prevention is both sound public health policy and sound economics.
Shri Gehlot emphasised the need to move beyond government-led programmes towards community-driven participation.
Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri B. L. Verma affirmed that the outcomes of the deliberations would inform the national action plan.
2. Accessible Scholarships, Empowered Students
Chaired by Shri Asim Arun, Minister in the Government of Uttar Pradesh, and co-chaired by Shri Kishan Kumar Bedi, Minister in the Government of Haryana, the session focused on developing an integrated, accessible and student-centric scholarship delivery ecosystem.
The deliberations emphasized simplification of application procedures, secure digital integration between the Centre and States, assisted application facilities, timely disbursement of scholarships and strengthened grievance redressal mechanisms. Suggestions relating to revision of income eligibility criteria and scholarship amounts were also discussed.
States highlighted successful initiatives, including common scholarship platforms in Odisha, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh; Andhra Pradesh’s One Stop Scholarship Portal; prior scrutiny of applications in Madhya Pradesh; and auto-approval mechanisms adopted by Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
The discussions underscored the importance of technology-enabled service delivery, intergovernmental coordination and transparent processes to ensure that eligible students receive scholarship assistance in a timely and hassle-free manner.
3. Early Intervention and Reduction of Disability Burden
The session, chaired by Dr. Shweta Gupta, Minister in the Government of Bihar, and co-chaired by Ms. Pi Lalrinpuii, Minister in the Government of Mizoram, focused on strengthening early identification, timely assessment and intervention for children with developmental delays and disabilities.
The key priorities included strengthening convergence among health, nutrition, education and disability-related services; expanding tele-rehabilitation and mobile outreach facilities; developing integrated digital tracking systems; and enhancing the availability of trained human resources.
West Bengal presented its SANSPARSH model, which facilitates community-level screening for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) through a 20-point questionnaire.
Dr. Gupta highlighted that early identification and convergence of existing services are critical to reducing the burden of disability and ensuring that support reaches beneficiaries at the grassroots level.
Ms. Lalrinpuii emphasised the importance of parental awareness, continuous follow-up and shared responsibility among families, institutions and service providers.
4. Sugamya Bharat for Viksit Bharat
The fourth thematic session focused on mainstreaming universal accessibility and inclusive design in public infrastructure, transport systems and digital services from the planning stage itself. The discussions highlighted the need for regular accessibility audits, effective monitoring mechanisms and active participation of persons with disabilities in the design and evaluation of public facilities.
States showcased several good practices, including Kochi Metro and Water Metro in Kerala, with Indian Sign Language-trained staff and accessible amenities; accessibility upgrades at Chennai Egmore and suburban railway stations in Tamil Nadu, including Braille-enabled lifts, tactile pathways and induction loops; accessible tourist spaces in Goa; level-boarding Ahmedabad Janmarg buses in Gujarat; and mandatory barrier-free infrastructure in schools in Assam.
Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri B. L. Verma emphasised that accessibility is not an additional facility but the foundation of equal opportunities and a life of dignity, particularly in the context of the national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.
Goa Minister Shri Subhash Faldessai advocated incorporating accessibility at the design and planning stage rather than relying on retrofitting.
Assam highlighted proposals for a dedicated National Mission, district-level monitoring and appropriate penalties for non-compliance with accessibility requirements.
Knowledge-sharing and exhibition of best practices
During the full-house sessions, experts Dr. Varsha Gathoo (formerly AYJNISHD) and Prof. J. S. Thakur (PGIMER) presented global best practices from the US, Australia, Switzerland, Iceland, Thailand, and the African Union alongside national policies.
An exhibition at Sushma Swaraj Bhawan showcased schemes, initiatives, success stories, digital applications and portals of both Departments, providing participants with an opportunity to understand innovative interventions and effective models of service delivery.
Renewed commitment to inclusive and empowered India
The deliberations culminated in a renewed commitment to strengthen Centre-State cooperation, institutional convergence and time-bound implementation of the agreed action points.
The Summit provided an important platform for translating policy priorities into coordinated action, leveraging successful State-level practices and addressing implementation gaps through collective responsibility.
With a shared focus on drug demand reduction, equitable access to educational opportunities, early intervention for persons with disabilities and universal accessibility, ‘SAMAVESHI NITI SANKALP 2026’ reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to building an inclusive, empowered, accessible and drug-free India in keeping with the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.

title: Data Users Conference on the New Series of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) to be held in Mumbai on 23rd November 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 6:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) is organising a “Data Users Conference on the New Series of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP)” on 23rd November 2026 in Mumbai. The conference follows the launch of the new series of all three indicators during the year 2026 and aims to familiarise data users with the methodological changes, data sources used and key improvements.
The new series of National Accounts with base year 2022-23 was released on 27th February 2026, followed by updation in August 2026 on incorporation of updated series of IIP and Producer Price Index (PPI). The new series has improved measurement of the private corporate and unincorporated sectors through greater use of MCA data, Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), and the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) data etc. Adoption of double deflation in manufacturing sector in addition to agriculture sector, integration of Supply and Use Tables in annual estimates and use of Proportional Denton method for benchmarking and that of GST data for quarterly estimates are the other key features.
The new CPI series with base year 2024 was released on 12th February 2026. It is based on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) 2023-24 and adopts the Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP) 2018. The basket has been expanded to 358 items, including 50 services, with prices collected from 1,465 rural and 1,395 urban markets across 434 towns, besides 12 online markets. Rural house rent has been included for the first time, and administrative and e-commerce data are used for items such as fuel, air fares, telecom charges and OTT services.
The new IIP series with base year 2022-23, aligned with the base year of GDP, WPI and PPI, was released on 1st June 2026. Its coverage has been expanded to include minor and rare earth minerals, gas supply, and a new sector of water supply, sewerage and waste management. The series has an updated item basket and factory panel, a provision for factory substitution, and greater use of the Output Producer Price Index (OPPI) for deflating production reported in value terms.
The conference will bring together representatives of RBI, SEBI, economists, researchers, experts from financial institutions and the banking sector, academia, subject-matter specialists, users of official statistics and senior officials from the Central Government.
The inaugural session will feature addresses by Dr. Saurabh Garg, Secretary, MoSPI; Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, RBI; Shri Deepak Parekh, Former Chairman, HDFC and Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics). It will be followed by three technical sessions on the new series of GDP, CPI and IIP, with presentations by MoSPI and RBI and open house discussions. A booklet containing the brief concept notes on the revised series of these indices will also be shared with the participants.
The conference will provide valuable opportunity to both users and official data compilers to directly discuss the changes, its interpretation and implications.
The conference aims to promote better understanding and effective use of official statistics and to strengthen engagement between MoSPI and the user community.
The Ministry welcomes active participation and insights of all stakeholders in this important consultative exercise.

content:
New Delhi, November 20, 2026:
Union Minister of Youth Affairs and Sports, Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya, inaugurated the 16th edition of TURF, FICCI’s (Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry) Global Summit on Business of Sports, in New Delhi on Friday.
Addressing the gathering, Dr. Mandaviya said, “Sports have emerged as a powerful instrument for youth development, social inclusion, economic opportunity and international cooperation.”
He said, “Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India has placed sports at the centre of its nation-building agenda. Our approach is guided by a clear vision – creating opportunities for every aspiring athlete, from the playground to the podium.”
The summit is being held under the theme “Powering India’s Sports Economy: Partnerships, Innovation & Global Leadership”.
Highlighting the transformation of India's sporting ecosystem over the last 12 years, Dr. Mandaviya said, “Through initiatives such as Khelo India Mission, Fit India Movement, and Target Olympic Podium Scheme, we are expanding grassroots participation, identifying sporting talent and creating pathways towards high-performance sports.”
The Union Cabinet recently approved the new Khelo India Scheme, with an outlay of Rs 36,441 crore for the next five years, to strengthen sports infrastructure, nurture talent, and promote sports development across the country.
Highlighting India's performance, Dr. Mandaviya said, “At the Asian Games 2026, India finished fourth in the medal standings.”
He added, “Equally historic was India's performance at the Asian Para Games 2026, where our para-athletes secured a record 114 medals, our highest-ever tally at the Games.”
Speaking on the role of industry, Dr. Mandaviya said, “We recognise that the future of sports will be shaped, not only by athletes and sporting institutions, but also by a strong, competitive and innovation-driven sports industry.”
The Government has approved the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme, with an outlay of Rs 1,856.67 crore, to make India a global hub for sports goods manufacturing and innovation.
Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 sets out a comprehensive vision for sports development in India, while the National Sports Governance Act is ensuring accountability and transparency in sports administration.
Dr. Mandaviya outlined India’s intent to host major international sporting events. India is set to host the Commonwealth Games 2030 in Ahmedabad, while also harbouring hopes of hosting the 2036 Olympics in the same city.
“In the last 18 months alone, India has successfully hosted 40 international sporting competitions across 18 cities, demonstrating not only the strength of our sporting infrastructure but also our growing organisational capabilities.”
The Union Sports Minister encouraged industry leaders to take a long-term strategic view of the sector. He said, “There is huge potential in developing sports infrastructure, high-performance academies, sports science facilities, sports technology, and athlete-management systems. Private investment can bring greater efficiency, innovation, and international best practices into our sporting ecosystem.
“Our vision is to transform India from a sporting nation into a global sports economy. As we move towards becoming a developed country by 2047, sports will play an important part in this journey,” said Dr. Mandaviya. He invited international partners, investors, manufacturers, and sporting institutions to partake in this transformation. “Let us work together to Make in India, Play in India, and Grow with India,” he said.
The inaugural session was attended by Shri P.K.S.V. Sagar, Chairman, FICCI Sports Committee and Strategic Advisor, GMR Group; Shri Sanjay Adesara, Co-Chairman, FICCI Sports Committee and Chief Business Officer, Adani Sportsline; Shri Vijay Shankar, President, FICCI; and Ms. Jyoti Vij, Director General, FICCI, along with international partners, sports leaders, industry representatives and athletes.

title: Putting AI to work for India’s MSMEs: Microsoft, Samhita-Collective Good Foundation, alongside Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog bring leaders together on 20 November
subtitle: Microsoft India and Samhita-CGF, alongside Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog convened to discuss the path towards AI enablement for India’s MSME sector, and the ecosystem-level support required to help them grow.
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 5:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
NEW DELHI, 20 November 2026:
AI is revolutionising every aspect of how we work and what productivity looks like. To ensure that India’s 10 crore MSMEs remain ahead of the curve in this moment of unprecedented technological transformation, Microsoft India and Samhita-CGF convened with Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog for the
AI Enablement for MSMEs Leadership Dialogue.
The convening brought together Dr. Deepak Bagla, Mission Director, Atal Innovation Mission, NITI Aayog; and Mr. Sanjay Chadha, General Manager, Corporate, External and Legal Affairs (CELA), Microsoft India & South Asia; alongside MSME founders and ecosystem partners. They discussed the state of AI adoption among India’s MSMEs, opportunities AI can unlock in economic growth and employment generation in the sector, and what an ecosystem-wide support system for MSME AI adoption can look like.
The dialogue was part of Microsoft’s AI Enablement for MSMEs initiative, which is helping 3,000 MSMEs in Andhra Pradesh, Delhi-NCR, Karnataka and Maharashtra adopt AI workflows across business functions over a 60-day AI learning journey to become more efficient, productive and scalable.
“India’s next leap of growth depends on how we democratize AI, so that even the smallest businesses can adopt it without the barriers of expertise, time and cost. The biggest delta advantage in value creation from AI will come from our MSMEs and the self-employed. Their aim is not just to create financial unicorns but also to create social unicorns by impacting over a billion lives,” said Dr. Bagla
.
At the event, Microsoft India, and Samhita-CGF, the program delivery partner, unveiled a
multilingual AI chatbot
available in the regional languages of the MSMEs and designed to help them continue learning and applying AI in their daily operations after the training ends. The chatbot is soon going to be scaled to support MSMEs across the country.
“India's Digital Public Infrastructure brought millions of MSMEs into the digital economy. In the age of AI, the next frontier is productivity. When small businesses adopt AI with the right skills and the trust that it is being used responsibly, their people do higher-value work, firms grow and new jobs follow. We are working with India's incubation network to help MSMEs move from AI awareness to adoption, and to make responsible AI the foundation of lasting economic mobility," said Sanjay Chadha, General Manager, Corporate, External and Legal Affairs (CELA), Microsoft India & South Asia.
Microsoft and Samhita-CGF are also planning a
National MSME AI Adoption Playbook
, drawing on insights from the learning experiences of 6,000 individuals participating in the program. The Playbook will capture practical approaches, success stories and insights to help industry associations, incubators and government institutions support AI adoption at scale.
"The timing is right. Generative AI now sits inside everyday productivity tools, India's AI infrastructure is expanding, and larger enterprises are raising digital expectations for MSMEs. This initiative could not have come at a better time. I am thankful to Microsoft for being the pillar that is bringing together capacity building, thought leadership, systems-level approach and meaningful collaboration with the government and enabling the success of this initiative" said Ms. Priya Naik, CEO, Samhita-CGF.

India's agricultural exports recorded strong growth during April-September FY 2026-27, led by Basmati rice, processed frozen potatoes and yellow dent corn. Basmati rice exports increased 25.4%, while processed potato exports rose 20.8%. Yellow dent corn exports surged around 12-fold. Strong growth in exports across West Asia, East and Southeast Asia, and other international markets reflects the widening geographical reach of India's agricultural and processed food exports.
Introduction
India's agricultural exports recorded strong growth
across key commodities during April–September FY 2026–27, with Basmati rice, prepared or preserved frozen potatoes and yellow dent corn registering significant increases. Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Yemen and Oman.
The
United States

East and Southeast Asia, particularly in Indonesia, and Japan.
Yellow dent corn registered a particularly sharp increase in exports, with
Vietnam, Bangladesh and the Philippines
emerging as major destinations. Growth across these agricultural commodities highlights the widening geographical spread of India's exports and its expanding presence in international markets.

title: India’s Television Broadcasting Shift
subtitle: Tracing the transition from Analogue to Digital TV Broadcasting
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 12:01PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Setting the Context: World Television Day
Broadcasting
is the systematic transmission of audio and video content to a large audience through electronic communication networks.
Television broadcasting
combines sound and moving images to deliver news, information, education and entertainment. Over the decades, technological advancements have expanded its reach through terrestrial, satellite, cable and internet-based platforms. This has made television an important medium of mass communication.
In India, television broadcasting has transformed communication by connecting diverse communities across geographical and linguistic boundaries. It has supported
socio-economic
development
through educational programmes, agricultural information, health awareness and public service campaigns.
It has also emerged as a major
source of entertainment,
bringing films, television serials, and sports etc. into millions of households, while also promoting India's cultural and linguistic diversity
.
It has further strengthened
public administration
by enabling the dissemination of government policies, welfare schemes, development initiatives and emergency information, thereby improving public awareness and access to essential information.
Recognising television's growing influence on public opinion, global communication and cultural exchange, the
United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 21 November as World Television Day in 1996
.
The observance recognises television's role in informing, educating and connecting societies. It also highlights the importance of responsible broadcasting in addressing contemporary challenges and supporting informed public discourse.
A television screen can bring distant events, new ideas and different perspectives into people's homes. It connects audiences with developments beyond their immediate surroundings. Over the decades, television has become an important medium for entertainment, information, education and public communication in India.
The Changing Technologies of Television
Television broadcasting in India has evolved alongside advances in
communication and transmission technologies
. Each technological advancement transformed the transmission and distribution of television programmes, expanding their reach and accessibility.
The Early Broadcast Era: Terrestrial Television (1959–1975)
India's television journey began with an experimental
broadcast in Delhi on 15 September 1959
. The initiative was launched by
All India Radio (AIR) under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
. A makeshift studio transmitted programmes through a small transmitter. Initially, broadcasts reached a
limited area around Delhi. The experiment evolved into a
regular television service in 1965
. Doordarshan began daily transmissions of daily Hindi News Bulletin on
15 August 1965
. By 1972, services were extended to Mumbai and Amritsar and then on to seven other cities by 1975. All this time,
it was part of the national broadcaster, All India Radio. On April 1, 1976, it transited to become a separate Department in the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
Click to Read More: Doordarshan's Legacy
Television broadcasting during this period relied primarily on
analogue terrestrial transmission
. This system used ground-based transmitters to send television signals through radio waves. Transmitters broadcast signals from antennas installed on elevated towers. Household television sets received these signals through indoor or outdoor antennas.
However, terrestrial broadcasting had
geographical and technical limitations.
Signal reception depended on the distance between households and transmitters. Hills, buildings and other physical obstructions could weaken or block signals. Consequently, reception quality varied across locations.
Analogue transmission also had
limited channel capacity
. Each assigned television frequency channel generally carried one programme. Expanding services therefore required additional frequencies, transmitters and supporting infrastructure. These constraints contributed to the gradual expansion of television services across the country.
Extending television beyond the reach of terrestrial transmitters required a different technological approach.
Satellite communication offered the possibility of transmitting television signals across much larger geographical areas
. This paved the way for satellite-based broadcasting and a wider national television network.
Satellite and Colour Broadcasting: Expanding Television's Reach (1975–1988)
The mid-1970s marked a turning point in India's television history. By 1976, India’s terrestrial network had eight stations covering
45 million people across 75,000 square kilometres
. Satellite technology and colour broadcasting transformed television's reach and viewing experience. Two major developments accelerated this expansion, taking television beyond urban centres.
The first major breakthrough was the
Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE),
conducted between August 1975 and July 1976. It used
satellite technology to broadcast educational programmes
directly to villages across six States. The experiment aimed to use television for education and socio-economic development. SITE demonstrated how satellite technology could overcome geographical barriers. It established television's potential as an instrument of education and public communication.
The next major development came with the introduction of the
Indian National Satellite (INSAT) system
.
INSAT-1A, launched on April 1982
, was India's
first-generation operational domestic communications satellite
. This enabled a common programme feed from Delhi to regional stations across the country. However, INSAT-1A was abandoned in 1983.
INSAT-1B,
launched in August 1983, strengthened this emerging national broadcasting network. It achieved full operational capability in October 1983. The satellite supported television broadcasting and other communication services. It helped consolidate satellite-based connectivity across Doordarshan's regional stations.
Did You Know?
Alongside satellite expansion, colour broadcasting transformed the television viewing experience. Doordarshan's first colour telecast took place on 15 August 1982, coinciding with the launch of its National Programme. Later that year, colour television gained wider public visibility through the live coverage of the Asian Games in New Delhi in November 1982. This milestone marked a shift from black-and-white transmissions to colour broadcasting.
Unlike terrestrial broadcasting, which relies on ground-based transmitters with geographically limited coverage, satellite communication enables television signals to reach much wider areas. A single satellite can serve multiple regions through its communication footprint. This capability helped extend television services to remote and previously underserved areas.
A satellite communication system has two main components: the
ground segment
and the
space segment
. The ground segment comprises Earth stations and associated transmission and reception equipment. The space segment consists of the satellite and its onboard transponders, which receive and retransmit communication signals.
The broadcasting process involves three stages. First,
the uplink transmits the television signal from an Earth station to the satellite.
The Earth station sends the signal towards the satellite using an uplink frequency.
The satellite's transponder receives the signal
, amplifies it and converts it to a different frequency. It then retransmits the signal towards Earth through the
downlink.
Next, receiving Earth stations capture the downlinked signal.
The signal is then distributed to television transmitters or cable distribution networks for delivery to viewers. A dish antenna at the subscriber's premises receives the satellite signal directly. Thus, satellite communication provides the long-distance link, while terrestrial transmitters and cable networks can support its final distribution.
This combination of satellite connectivity and colour broadcasting transformed India's television landscape. It expanded television's geographical reach and enhanced the viewing experience. The next phase brought private satellite television channels in the early 1990s. From the mid-1990s, cable television networks further expanded viewing choices in Indian households.
Did You Know?
A satellite’s
footprint
is the area on Earth where its signal can be received. A dish placed anywhere inside that area can pick up the satellite’s broadcast. A dish outside it gets a weak signal or none.
The Multi-Channel Era: Cable and Satellite Television (1990–2005)
This period witnessed a major transformation in India's television landscape. International satellite channels began reaching Indian audiences, starting with CNN. The launch of Star TV and Zee TV further accelerated the growth of satellite television. Domestic broadcasters, including Sun TV, also entered the emerging multi-channel market.
The arrival of satellite channels gave cable television a major boost. Broadcasters transmitted programme signals to satellites through uplinks. Satellites retransmitted these signals towards Earth, where local cable operators received them using dish antennas at their head ends. Operators then processed and organised the channels before distributing them to households through cable networks. Satellite technology enabled long-distance transmission, while cable networks facilitated local distribution. This combination brought a wider range of news, entertainment, sports and regional-language programming into Indian homes, beyond the reach of Doordarshan's terrestrial services.
However, cable television depended on physical infrastructure to connect operators with households. Extending these networks to remote and geographically challenging areas could be difficult. Direct-to-Home (DTH) broadcasting emerged as an alternative distribution platform. Unlike cable television, DTH delivers satellite signals directly to a dish antenna installed at the subscriber's premises.
Direct-to-Home and Digital Broadcasting (2003–2017)
The next phase of India's television evolution was marked by the expansion of DTH services and the transition from analogue to digital broadcasting. Dish TV launched India's first commercial DTH service in October 2003. In December 2004, Prasar Bharati launched Doordarshan's DD Direct Plus, now known as DD Free Dish. It introduced a free-to-air DTH platform that did not require a monthly subscription. These developments expanded access to satellite television, including in areas with limited cable connectivity.
DTH broadcasting delivers television signals directly from satellites to individual households, without requiring a local cable network. Broadcasters first convert television content into digital signals and compress them for efficient transmission.
These signals are transmitted to satellites using designated radio frequencies, generally in the Ku-band.
Satellites receive and retransmit these signals towards Earth over designated coverage areas.
Small dish antennas
installed at subscribers' premises receives these signals. A
digital set-top box processes the received signals
, decodes the selected content and makes television channels available for viewing. Subscription-based services use encryption and authorised access systems to restrict viewing to subscribed channels. In contrast,
free-to-air services, such as DD Free Dish, do not require a monthly subscription
.
What is Ku-band?
Satellite-based television services use specific portions of the radio frequency spectrum to transmit signals between satellites and Earth. The
Ku-band
is one such frequency band, commonly used for Direct-to-Home (DTH) broadcasting. It generally operates in the frequency range of 12–18 GHz. DTH services commonly use frequencies around 10.7–12.75 GHz for downlink transmission, depending on the system and regional allocation. Its relatively high frequencies allow the use of smaller dish antennas at subscriber premises. However, Ku-band signals can be affected by heavy rainfall, which may temporarily interrupt reception.
Modern Broadcasting: Emerging Technologies and New Frontiers (2018–Present)
Since 2018, India's broadcasting landscape has transformed with expanding internet connectivity, digital platforms and connected devices. Television viewing is no longer limited to conventional television sets or scheduled programmes. Viewers can access content through
smartphones, computers and Smart TVs.
Over-the-top (OTT)
platforms have enabled on-demand viewing across devices and locations. In November 2024,
Prasar Bharati
launched
WAVES
, its OTT digital streaming platform, bringing public service broadcasting content to digital audiences.
By November 2026, WAVES had recorded about 1.6 crore registered users.
Click to Read More About: WAVES OTT
Unlike conventional terrestrial broadcasting, which transmits television signals from ground-based towers to receiving antennas, and satellite broadcasting, which relays signals through communication satellites to receiving dishes,
OTT platforms deliver audio and video content through the internet.
Content is hosted on servers in data centres and accessed through broadband connectivity. Content Delivery Networks use geographically distributed servers to cache content closer to users. This helps reduce latency and improves content delivery.
Click to Read More:
Data Centres in India
;
Cloud Ecosystem in India
Another emerging technology is
Direct-to-Mobile (D2M) broadcasting
. It uses terrestrial infrastructure to transmit video, audio and data directly to compatible mobile devices. Reception does not require a SIM card or mobile data connection. Unlike OTT streaming, D2M uses broadcast transmission to reach multiple devices simultaneously.
Did You Know?
Prasar Bharati signed an MoU with IIT Kanpur to develop a next-generation broadcasting roadmap. A proof of concept for D2M broadcasting was subsequently completed by IIT Kanpur. Trials also examined hybrid transmission using High Power High Tower (HPHT) and Low Power Low Tower (LPLT) transmitters. In November 2025, Prasar Bharati published test results covering telecom interference and the thermal impact of D2M reception on mobile devices. The tests included an ATSC 3.0-based broadcast system.
Shaping the future of Broadcasting
India’s television ecosystem has grown from a single experimental service into a diverse, multi-platform network.
Doordarshan now runs 35 channels, up from 17 in 2010
.
[1]
DD Free Dish carries 482 channels, including educational ones, up from 59
[2]
.
Private satellite television has expanded from 603 channels in 2010–11 to 917 permitted channels as of March 2026. Of these, 908 channels were available for downlinking in India, comprising 342 pay channels and 566 free-to-air (FTA) channels. Of the pay channels, 238 were standard-definition (SD) and 104 were high-definition (HD) channels
[3]
. Private pay DTH serves 49.05 million active subscribers as on 31st March 2026. Doordarshan's DTH service provides 100% geographical and population coverage across the country
[4]
.
Collectively, terrestrial, satellite, cable, DTH and digital platforms bring television to urban, rural and remote homes.
The future of broadcasting will increasingly be shaped by technological convergence and expanding digital access.
High-definition transmission, digital delivery and internet-based platforms are transforming how audiences’ access and experience content. Broadcasting is also moving beyond conventional television networks towards more flexible and connected delivery systems. Public and private broadcasters will continue to play an important role in this transition. With expanding infrastructure, technological innovation and wider platform integration, India’s broadcasting ecosystem is evolving to serve diverse audiences and changing viewing preferences. These developments are shaping a more accessible, connected and future-ready broadcasting landscape.

title: NHRC, India takes suo motu cognizance of the reported transportation of the dead bodies of a woman and her daughter in a garbage vehicle for post-mortem after hospital staff failed to provide a hearse in Faridabad, Haryana
subtitle:
The Commission reiterates right to life, fair treatment and dignity under Article 21 also extends to the dead; reaffirms its 2021 Advisory on their respectful treatment

Issues notices to the Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare, Government of Haryana and District Magistrate, Faridabad, calling for detailed reports on the matter within two weeks
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                20 NOV 2026 1:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken
suo motu
cognizance of a media report that the dead bodies of a woman and her daughter were carried in a garbage vehicle from a hospital to the mortuary of Civil Hospital, Ballabhgarh in Haryana for post-mortem examination. They had succumbed to their injuries caused in a road accident in the Ballabhgarh area of Faridabad on 14
th
November 2026. Reportedly, the hospital staff failed to provide their family members with a hearse to carry the bodies.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of human rights. The right to life and human dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution of India extends to the deceased, requiring authorities and institutions to treat dead bodies with respect.
